Minimum-effort carousel built only from the verified 10-23 Short script, with no new research. Drop it if that script isn't confirmed as verified.
Slides:
(1) The worry, named as understandable.
(2) 10 pooled studies, 660 people on semaglutide: no clear change in average handgrip strength, exactly as verified.
(3) Very low certainty and studies that varied a lot.
(4) Lean mass (weight) is not the same as strength (function).
(5) The SURMOUNT-1 body-scan anchor (tirzepatide; adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes; 72 weeks), exactly as verified.
(6) Recommended habits, not proven on the drug: a protein food at each meal unless your clinician has told you to limit protein (for example, kidney disease), and muscle-strengthening at least 2 days a week, started gently.
(7) Common GI side effects, 'don't stop or change your medicines on your own', 'Not personal advice' and the full prescriber line.
No emoji.

package.title: Does Semaglutide Weaken Your Grip? What a New Review Shows

social.instagram_caption:
Worried semaglutide might weaken your grip? Fair thing to wonder.

A new meta-analysis (Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism, online Oct 19, 2026) pooled 10 studies and 660 adults on semaglutide, comparing grip strength before and after treatment (no control group). The average result: no clear change.

But here's the nuance:
→ The review rated its certainty very low, and results varied a lot between studies
→ Lean mass (what a body scan measures) isn't the same as strength (what grip and function tests measure)
→ In a separate tirzepatide trial (SURMOUNT-1 body-scan subgroup: 160 adults — 124 on tirzepatide, all doses pooled, and 36 on placebo; obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes), people lost more fat and more lean mass than on placebo over 72 weeks, but strength wasn't measured

Bottom line: the evidence can't yet tell whether semaglutide changes grip strength.

General habits that help protect muscle (not proven on these medicines specifically): a protein food at each meal, unless your clinician told you to limit protein (for example, kidney disease); muscle-strengthening activity 2+ days a week, starting gently; and asking your prescriber to help you plan.

Common side effects of both medicines include feeling sick, diarrhoea, vomiting and constipation (NHS). Don't stop or change your medicines on your own.

Save this for your next appointment, and send it to the friend who asked.

#Semaglutide #Tirzepatide #GLP1 #MuscleHealth #GripStrength #MetabolicHealth

Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

slides.headline: Worried semaglutide will weaken your grip?
slides.bubble: Honestly? Totally fair thing to wonder.

slides.headline: Adults on semaglutide across 10 grip studies (before-and-after data only)
slides.body: Across 10 pooled studies, average handgrip strength in adults on semaglutide showed no clear change from before to after treatment. The analysis compared people with themselves before and after treatment, not with a control group (Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism meta-analysis, online Oct 19, 2026).

slides.headline: MYTH: This proves grip strength is unaffected
slides.body: FACT: The review rated its certainty very low. Results varied a lot between studies, and the pooled data were before-and-after changes with no control group. The authors say the evidence can't yet tell whether semaglutide changes grip strength. More research is needed.

slides.headline: Lean mass is not the same as strength
slides.body: Losing lean mass on a scan doesn't automatically mean losing strength. They measure different things.
slides.bubble: Plot twist: lean mass isn't all muscle!

Separate trial from the semaglutide grip review. Strength not measured.

factcheck.summary: The carousel is accurate, careful and safe. I confirmed the key source through the NCBI E-utilities record for PMID 42897109: Machado LG et al., Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism, published online ahead of print on 19 Oct 2026, DOI 10.1111/dom.71432. It reports 10 studies and 660 people treated with semaglutide. The pooled change in handgrip strength was -0.16 kgf (95% CI -1.98 to 1.65), which is not significant. Heterogeneity was substantial and certainty very low. The authors say the evidence is 'insufficient to determine whether semaglutide is associated with changes in handgrip strength'. The hook, the stat slide, the MYTH/FACT slide and the CTA all keep to that scope, and the title is paid off. The tirzepatide numbers on slide 5 (160 people: 124 on tirzepatide, all doses pooled, and 36 on placebo; fat mass -33.9% vs -8.2%, lean mass -10.9% vs -2.6% at week 72) match the SURMOUNT-1 body-composition paper (Look et al., DOM 2025). That slide also states the population, says it's a separate trial and says strength wasn't measured. The safety caveats are in place: the kidney-disease caveat on protein, 'start gently' for exercise, no stopping or changing medicines on your own, and the disclaimer plus the prescriber line on the last slide. The WHO 2020 guideline and both NHS medicine pages exist and support the claims. Four minor wording and sourcing fixes are listed below.

issues.location: Slide 2 (stat) headline and body; Slide 3 (myth_fact) body
issues.claim: '(no placebo group)' and 'Most studies had no comparison group'
issues.problem: The abstract says the review included randomized, non-randomized and uncontrolled studies, and that the pooled analysis used within-group (before-and-after) changes. I couldn't verify 'most studies'. It's the analysis that had no control comparison, and some of the included trials may have had control arms.
issues.fix: Slide 2 headline: 'Adults on semaglutide across 10 grip studies (before-and-after data only)'. Slide 2 body, last sentence: 'The analysis compared people with themselves before and after treatment, not with a control group (Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism meta-analysis, online Oct 19, 2026).' Slide 3 body: replace 'and most had no comparison group' with 'and the pooled data were before-and-after changes with no control group'.

issues.claim: Lean mass lost: 10.9% on tirzepatide vs 2.6% on placebo, in 160 adults (124 vs 36)
issues.problem: These exact figures, including the lean-mass percentages and the 124/36 split, come from the SURMOUNT-1 body-composition paper (Look et al., DOM 2025). The main NEJM paper (S2) doesn't clearly report all of them in its main text.
issues.fix: Add a source: 'S6: Body composition changes during weight reduction with tirzepatide in the SURMOUNT-1 study of adults with obesity or overweight. Look M et al. Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism, published Feb 25, 2025. DOI 10.1111/dom.16275. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11965027/'. Credit slide 5's numbers to S6 (with S2 for the trial itself).

issues.problem: The NHS pages list the common side effects without ranking them. Feeling tired, injection-site reactions and hair loss are listed too, so 'the most common' says more than the source does.
issues.fix: Replace with: 'For semaglutide and tirzepatide, common side effects include stomach-related ones (NHS). Don't stop or change your medicines on your own: ask your prescriber what helps.'

issues.problem: NHS lists vomiting as common with both medicines. The other cards say 'Common with both medicines', so this card is less consistent. The prescriber advice is fine.
issues.fix: Detail: 'Common with both. Tell your prescriber if it keeps happening'.
